thread.title: Chrysler Expands U.S. Minivan Market Share From 51% To 57% - Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (NYSE:FCAU)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: Chrysler Expands U.S. Minivan Market Share From 51% To 57% - Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (NYSE:FCAU)
text:
There are some subjects in the automotive industry that are bordering on taboo. One of them is that brand new regular gasoline cars in the U.S. are extremely clean, and that’s why the air in the U.S. has been getting cleaner every year for many years already, and will continue to get cleaner every year into the future, even if emissions standards don’t tighten at all going forward.
Another taboo in the automotive industry is minivans. From their 1984 instant hit with Chrysler-Dodge ( FCAU ), they have become as talked-about in polite circles as calling your baby ugly. Nobody wants to bring up the minivan subject anymore.
But today, we are breaking this silent treatment. This Christmas, we are talking about that 800 pound baby gorilla-elephant sitting in the middle of the living room, right in front of the Christmas tree.
And we are going to talk about it, because I have found some numbers for you. Specifically, I have the U.S. minivan sales numbers for January-November 2018, compared to what they were one year prior.
These numbers show some surprising results. They also call for predictions about the new vehicle planning, that we should expect to see on the road in 2019, 2020 and 2021. I will discuss those future market shifts, and why the U.S. minivan market looks to take a surprising turn in 2022. Yes, 2022.

As you can see in the table above, we have some difficulty eyeballing the analysis. There’s visual noise in the table, that we really ought to fix -- but also one thing that we must keep as part of the critical analysis.
First, the Chrysler Town & Country was phased out already in 2016, with essentially zero sales in 2017. It must be filtered out. Second, the Nissan ( OTCPK:NSANY ) Quest was phased out in 2017, and only had a 1% market share to begin with, so it too needs to be essentially disregarded.
However, there is one thing about this table that stands out above all others: The Dodge Caravan. At 142,233 units sold in the U.S. for the first eleven months of 2018, it is not only up a whopping 20%, but it has gained 5% market share to an impressive 32% total.
This is for a product which is seemingly hopelessly out of date, as it was first shown in 2007, making it one of the very oldest design in the U.S. car market right now. It was “replaced” in the first half of 2016 by the significantly modernized Chrysler Pacifica -- except FCA kept manufacturing the old model, the Dodge Caravan, to this date. It obviously outsells its intended successor product thanks to one simple factor: Price.
One would reasonably have believed that the sales of the Dodge Caravan would have dropped to a trickle, already by the end of 2016, but no, that didn’t happen at all. U.S. sales of the old Caravan have remained very strong, and its 20% increase in 2018 is one of the greater mysteries in the entire U.S. automotive market.
Let’s put this 142,233 unit sales number of this almost prehistoric minivan model into perspective, by comparing it with Tesla’s U.S. sales number for the same time period. The point with this comparison is to consider the amount of attention Tesla ( TSLA ) gets for its U.S. sales numbers, especially the launch of the Model 3, which in 2018 sold only in the U.S. and Canada -- not yet in Europe or Asia.

As you can see in the table above, FCA’s market dominance becomes even clearer when you condense the table to the corporate parent level. FCA held a commanding 51% market share in 2017, but in amazing feat it managed to expand this to a whopping 57% in 2018.
Toyota ( TM ) was the biggest loser on an absolute unit basis. With a 21% sales decline, it lost an entire five points of market share, falling from 23% to 18%. The Sienna is the only minivan available with optional all-wheel drive (AWD), but the car is nearing the end of its generational replacement cycle. The seating position is a bit odd, and the infotainment system lacks basic features such as Android ( GOOGL ) Auto, which is a handicap in a world where approximately 85% of the world’s smartphone population uses Android.
The Sienna’s exterior design has held up very well, its cockpit is super-easy to use, and it continues to hold a well-deserved stellar quality reputation, but apparently that was not enough for the U.S. market in 2018. Contrary to Toyota’s excellent hybrid heritage, it offers relatively unimpressive fuel economy at 18 MPG city, 27 MPG highway -- which is no match for Chrysler’s Pacifica hybrid, which is rated at 30 MPG combined city/highway.
The other market share loser is the Kia ( OTCPK:HYMLF ) Sedona, which was already the smallest player not (yet) exiting the U.S. minivan market. It lost 25% of its U.S. sales in 2018, and is now down to 4% market share. The exterior design remains not only fresh, but great-looking in my opinion -- however it gets dinged for other shortcomings.
Specifically, the Sedona is slightly smaller than the other minivans, which is a problem when many consider size to be the whole point of having a minivan to begin with. In addition, the fuel economy is even less than the Toyota Sienna, at 18 MPG city and 24 MPG highway.
That leaves us with the other winner in the U.S. 2018 minivan market share race: Honda ( HMC ) Odyssey. It grew units sales 6% to go from 20% share to 22%. In doing that, it essentially swapped places with the Toyota Sienna in the market statistics.
The Honda Odyssey isn’t really much more fuel-efficient than the Toyota Sienna at 19 MPG city and 28 MPG highway, but it is a fresher design, that came out in the second quarter of 2017. The infotainment system also has not only Apple ( AAPL ) CarPlay, but also Android Auto -- two features now considered essential by many buyers.
Minivan predictions for 2019-2021 FCA will finally stop making the Dodge Caravan. It will be replaced by a slightly deconcented version of the Chrysler Pacifica, which will also see an after-discount price cut.
Toyota will replace the Sienna with a brand new generation, perhaps late 2019 or in 2020 at the latest. One generation later than it should have, it will probably include at least a hybrid variant, and probably a plug-in hybrid one too.
Honda: Nothing. Probably no drastic changes to the Odyssey, other than minor refresh-updates. Eventually, longer-term, perhaps a hybrid powertrain.
Kia: Will Kia stick with the minivan? I think so, but the answer is not obvious, and will depend on where sales go from here. It remains an important part of Kia’s portfolio for some non-U.S. markets, and even at 20,000 units per year in the U.S., it ought to play a role in Kia’s nameplate portfolio.
Major minivan market changes for 2022 Two things should change the minivan landscape dramatically in 2022:
Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAF ) will start producing the minivan version of its all-electric ( BEV ) platform, and the concept version is called “ID BUZZ.” This is the spiritual and de-facto successor to the “hippie van/bus” from the late 1960s. It could have a $110 kWh or larger battery, and a range of approximately 300 miles. All-wheel drive would be standard or at least optional. Price? A very non-hippie “expensive.”
Two years ago, in January 2017, Chrysler showed a concept of an all-electric ( BEV ) minivan. It is thought that Waymo ( GOOG ) helped prod FCA to go down this path. It also makes sense because of FCA’s 57% segment market share: If someone will have an all-electric minivan, it had better be FCA. It is unclear whether this minivan has been approved for production, but if it has -- we should expect volume deliveries by 2022.
One final note on market size With approximately 445,000 units sold in the U.S. for the first eleven months of 2018, and December usually being a seasonally strong sales month, we should be looking at approximately 500,000 minivan units sold for the year, in the U.S. It’s basically the same number as in 2017.
In a 17 million unit U.S. annual new light vehicle sales market, that means minivans fall just shy of 3% of the market. However, as we showed in the table above, on the other hand Tesla sold “only” 159,027 cars in the U.S. for the first eleven months of 2018. Add another estimated 26,000 U.S. Teslas for December, and the year would come to 185,000 sold in the U.S.
So, 500,000 annual minivan sales in the U.S., vs approximately 185,000 cars sold by Tesla in the U.S. Which of these categories gets the most attention? And which of these will endure with profitability in 2019 and 2020?
